Implementation-relevant•Peer-reviewed prospective multicenter cross-sectional validation study•September 21, 2026

Five-class tau PET framework detects more early pathology

In 681 participants, a five-class visual framework achieved interrater kappa values of 0.77 to 0.85 and classified more cognitively unimpaired and MCI participants as tau-positive than the FDA-approved flortaucipir binary read, but the new framework itself is not authorized or guideline-endorsed and has no proven clinical utility.

Key quantitative results: Interrater agreement for the five classes was kappa 0.77 to 0.85. Intertracer agreement was highest for MK-6240 versus flortaucipir (kappa 0.88); across all tracer pairs, five-class percentage agreement ranged from 75.2% to 83.3%.

BiomarkersTau PETTau tanglesAmyloidTau pathology staging

Added September 22, 2026 · DOI:10.1001/jamaneurol.2026.3253; PMID:42766299

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The harmonized approach moves tau PET beyond a late-stage binary read and provides a common vocabulary across four tracers. It increases early-stage positivity and tracks with cognition and other biomarkers, but the same cohort was used to develop and evaluate it, and no prospective decision-impact or outcome study has established clinical utility.

Study design

The HEAD study enrolled adults aged 50 to 90 years at nine North American and European sites. The analysis included 681 participants (369 cognitively unimpaired, 245 with MCI and 67 with dementia) who underwent two to four tau PET scans, amyloid PET, MRI and cognitive assessment. Blinded readers assigned negative, low, moderate, high or atypical classes from seven composite regions.

Key quantitative results

  • Interrater agreement for the five classes was kappa 0.77 to 0.85. Intertracer agreement was highest for MK-6240 versus flortaucipir (kappa 0.88); across all tracer pairs, five-class percentage agreement ranged from 75.2% to 83.3%.
  • Among cognitively unimpaired participants, the FDA-approved flortaucipir binary read was positive in 26/364, versus 49/364 with harmonized flortaucipir (prevalence ratio 1.89, 95% CI 1.31 to 2.70) and 71/364 with harmonized MK-6240 (2.73, 1.95 to 3.83). In MCI, the corresponding counts were 100/223, 123/223 (1.23, 1.12 to 1.35) and 142/223 (1.42, 1.27 to 1.59).
  • From low to high tau classes, cognition was 1.4-fold worse, amyloid PET burden 3.2-fold higher and plasma p-tau217 2.5-fold higher; positivity estimates converged in dementia at 45/57, 47/57 and 50/57 for the regulatory, harmonized flortaucipir and harmonized MK-6240 reads.

What changed

A peer-reviewed prospective multicenter study now provides a reproducible five-class visual staging framework across four tau PET tracers and quantifies how much more early-stage pathology it detects than the approved flortaucipir binary read.

Strength of evidence

Strong agreement and convergent clinical-validity evidence within a large head-to-head imaging cohort. Analytical validity and reader reproducibility were not established outside the study, the framework was developed and evaluated in the same cohort, and longitudinal prognostic and decision-impact validation are still needed.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The framework may improve research staging and trial enrichment, especially before dementia, but it should not be substituted for an approved tracer's labeled read or used alone for treatment decisions until externally validated and implemented under appropriate guidance.

Field medical relevance

Directly relevant to imaging interpretation, biological staging and blood-biomarker studies that use tau PET as a reference. It also shows that tracer and reading method can change apparent positivity in early disease.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The method uses tracer-specific images but a common seven-region, five-class visual scheme. Agreement was strongest for MK-6240 and flortaucipir, and performance was lower for some regions with PI-2620, so tracer equivalence should not be assumed.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No new authorization, commercial availability, guideline endorsement, coverage or reimbursement follows from the framework. A free research visual-reading tool is available, but access to tracers, scanners and trained readers remains separate.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Is this five-class read FDA approved?
No. Tauvid and Tauklarify are approved tracers with their own labeled visual-read methods; this harmonized framework is a research method and has no separate authorization.
Does greater positivity prove better diagnosis or outcomes?
No. The study supports agreement and association with disease measures, but it did not establish that the additional early positives improve decisions, outcomes or treatment selection.
Can results be treated as interchangeable across tracers?
No. Agreement was good to excellent overall but varied by tracer and region, and atypical classifications did not converge across tracers.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Framework development and evaluation occurred in the same cohort without external validation
  • Cross-sectional design without longitudinal prognostic or treatment-response assessment
  • Smaller RO948 and PI-2620 samples and lower regional confidence for PI-2620
  • Predominantly highly educated White non-Hispanic academic-research cohort
  • No neuropathology reference standard, decision-impact study or clinical-utility evaluation

Primary source · DOI · JAMA Neurology full text · Research visual-reading tool

Benedet AL, et al; HEAD study. A Harmonized Visual Reading Framework for Tau PET Staging in Alzheimer Disease. JAMA Neurol. Published online September 21, 2026. doi:10.1001/jamaneurol.2026.3253.

Important new evidence•Peer-reviewed multicohort observational biomarker analysis•September 21, 2026

GFAP further stratifies decline among p-tau217-positive adults

Across 3,505 participants from six cohorts, co-elevated plasma GFAP and p-tau217 was associated with 62% faster annual CDR-SB progression and a 28% higher hazard of clinical worsening than p-tau217 positivity alone, supporting prognostic enrichment but not clinical utility.

Key quantitative results: Compared with p-tau217-positive/GFAP-negative participants, those positive for both biomarkers had a 62% faster annual CDR-SB progression rate (p=0.008).

BiomarkersBloodPlasma GFAPPlasma p-tau217Prognostic stratification

Added September 22, 2026 · DOI:10.1186/s13024-026-00995-5

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The study asks a clinically useful biomarker question: why people with elevated p-tau217 can follow different courses. GFAP added prognostic separation across multiple cohorts, but the association is observational, GFAP is nonspecific, thresholds were cohort-specific and the hazard ratio was modest with a lower confidence bound near 1.

Study design

Pooled analysis of 3,505 individuals across six independent cohorts spanning cognitively unimpaired aging through Alzheimer disease. All had baseline amyloid PET, plasma GFAP, plasma p-tau217 and CDR-SB. Four biomarker groups were followed for up to five years; models assessed baseline severity, annual CDR-SB change and time to a CDR-SB increase of at least 0.5 points.

Key quantitative results

  • Compared with p-tau217-positive/GFAP-negative participants, those positive for both biomarkers had a 62% faster annual CDR-SB progression rate (p=0.008).
  • Dual-positive participants had a higher hazard of clinical worsening, defined as a CDR-SB increase of at least 0.5 points (hazard ratio 1.28, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.61).
  • The GFAP-by-p-tau217 interaction accounted for 68.6% of biomarker-attributable variance in individual annual CDR-SB change, compared with 25.3% for p-tau217 and 1.1% for GFAP independent effects.

What changed

A large multicohort longitudinal analysis now quantifies how astrocyte-reactivity status may separate progression risk within the clinically heterogeneous p-tau217-positive population.

Strength of evidence

Moderate-to-strong clinical-validity evidence from six cohorts with amyloid PET and longitudinal outcomes. It remains observational, uses cohort- and assay-specific thresholds, does not establish incremental performance over full clinical models, and provides no prospective decision-impact or outcome evidence.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Dual GFAP and p-tau217 measurement may help enrich trials or identify research participants at greater progression risk, but this paper does not support a universal clinical cutoff or prove that management changes based on the combination improve outcomes.

Field medical relevance

Relevant to prognostic claims, trial enrichment and interpretation of a positive p-tau217 result. It separates added prognostic association from analytical validation, authorization and clinical utility.

Quanterix or platform relevance

GFAP and p-tau217 positivity was defined within cohort and assay rather than with a single clinically validated cross-platform threshold. The prognostic association therefore does not establish interchangeable cut points or transferability to a specific commercial assay.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No assay authorization, availability, guideline endorsement, coverage or reimbursement change follows from this report.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does GFAP diagnose Alzheimer disease?
No. GFAP reflects astrocyte reactivity and is not specific to Alzheimer disease; this analysis used it to stratify progression among groups defined with p-tau217 and amyloid PET.
Can one commercial cutoff be used from this study?
No. Assays and positivity definitions were cohort-specific, so the study does not establish a single transferable clinical threshold.
Is clinical utility established?
No. The study did not test whether acting on combined GFAP and p-tau217 results changes treatment decisions, counseling quality or patient outcomes.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Observational pooled analysis cannot establish that astrocyte reactivity causes faster decline
  • Cohort-specific assays and positivity thresholds limit direct cross-platform implementation
  • GFAP is biologically nonspecific and may reflect non-Alzheimer processes
  • The worsening hazard estimate was modest and its 95% confidence interval began at 1.01
  • No analytical-validation, prospective decision-impact or clinical-utility study

Primary source · DOI · Open-access full article

Bellaver B, Povala G, Ferreira PCL, et al; HEAD study. Astrocyte reactivity identifies p-tau217-positive individuals at elevated risk of cognitive decline across the Alzheimer's disease continuum. Mol Neurodegener. Published online September 21, 2026. doi:10.1186/s13024-026-00995-5.

Practice-relevant•Peer-reviewed randomized clinical trial and prespecified delayed-access follow-up•September 21, 2026

WeCareAdvisor yields modest caregiver benefits, not fewer behaviors

In 262 dementia caregivers, immediate WeCareAdvisor access did not significantly improve any of three prespecified outcomes at the three-month timepoint, but longitudinal distress and secondary wellbeing measures favored immediate use; delayed access produced fewer gains and one fewer DICE session.

Key quantitative results: At three months, none of the three prespecified timepoint comparisons was significant: behavior frequency-by-severity p=0.14, caregiver distress p=0.074 and confidence p=0.19. The longitudinal distress interaction was significant (Bonferroni-corrected p=0.012); post hoc distress fell 5.3 points with immediate versus 2.1 with delayed access, difference-in-differences 3.3 (95% CI 1.1 to 5.4; p=0.0031; Cohen d=0.386).

Clinical TrialsManagementCaregiver support

Added September 22, 2026 · NCT05012410; DOI:10.1093/geront/gnag226; PMID:42767991; supporting DOI:10.1111/jgs.70637

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

WeCareAdvisor operationalizes the DICE approach in a web app that tailors non-drug strategies to behavioral symptoms and possible triggers. The trial supports modest caregiver-distress and wellbeing gains, not a clear reduction in patient behaviors, and the new follow-up suggests that providing access earlier may improve engagement and the breadth of benefit.

Study design

A nationwide trial randomized 262 community-living caregivers of people with dementia to immediate access (n=131) or three-month delayed access (n=131). Masked interviewers assessed three primary outcomes and seven prespecified secondary outcomes through three months; the September 21 report compared engagement and outcomes after delayed users received access during months three to six.

Key quantitative results

  • At three months, none of the three prespecified timepoint comparisons was significant: behavior frequency-by-severity p=0.14, caregiver distress p=0.074 and confidence p=0.19. The longitudinal distress interaction was significant (Bonferroni-corrected p=0.012); post hoc distress fell 5.3 points with immediate versus 2.1 with delayed access, difference-in-differences 3.3 (95% CI 1.1 to 5.4; p=0.0031; Cohen d=0.386).
  • Caregiver wellbeing improved in 52% of immediate users versus 27% of delayed controls at three months (p=0.0003). Secondary outcomes also favored immediate use for wellbeing and upset with functional decline, but multiplicity was not controlled for these exploratory comparisons.
  • In the new delayed-access analysis, delayed users completed 3.1 DICE sessions versus 4.2 among immediate users (p=0.0052). Delayed users improved in wellbeing (p<0.001) and confidence (p=0.0069) but not behavioral symptoms (p>0.05), and immediate users improved more on most outcomes.

What changed

A peer-reviewed delayed-access analysis now completes the randomized trial's six-month comparison and shows that later access was associated with less engagement and fewer areas of improvement, while confirming no clear change in behavioral symptoms.

Strength of evidence

Randomized prospective evidence with masked interviewers and low three-month attrition, but the trial used a waitlist rather than active control, did not meet its three prespecified timepoint outcomes, relied on caregiver report and was demographically narrow. Secondary and post hoc findings require cautious interpretation.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The app may be a scalable adjunct for caregiver problem-solving and wellbeing, particularly when offered promptly, but it should not be presented as proven to reduce dementia-related behaviors or replace individualized clinical assessment of new or severe symptoms.

Field medical relevance

Directly relevant to supportive care, nonpharmacologic management and caregiver intervention discussions, including how timing and engagement affect real-world digital-tool benefit.

Access or reimbursement relevance

The publications establish no authorization, formal guideline endorsement, coverage or reimbursement policy. Public availability and implementation support for the app were not established by the trial reports.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Did the trial meet its primary outcomes?
Not at the prespecified three-month timepoint. The significant distress finding came from the longitudinal interaction, and the 3.3-point change contrast was a post hoc analysis.
Did the app reduce behavioral symptoms?
No clear timepoint benefit was shown for behavior frequency-by-severity, and delayed users also had no significant behavioral-symptom change after access.
Who was studied?
Community caregivers of people with dementia of varied etiologies; 67.9% were reported as Alzheimer disease and 32.1% as FTD, PPA or PSP. Most caregivers were female, White, highly educated and living with the person with dementia.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • No significant immediate-versus-delayed difference for any of the three prespecified primary outcomes at the three-month timepoint
  • Waitlist control without an attention-matched digital comparator
  • Caregiver-reported outcomes and no blinded participant exposure
  • Predominantly White, female and college-educated caregiver sample with internet access
  • Mixed dementia etiologies and exploratory secondary analyses without multiplicity adjustment

Primary source · DOI · Primary three-month randomized trial report · ClinicalTrials.gov record · PubMed record

Gitlin LN, McClure LA, Webster MJ, Lyketsos C, Kales HC. Timing Matters: Effects of Delayed versus Immediate Access to a Web-Based Application on Caregiver Outcomes: The WeCareAdvisor Trial. Gerontologist. Published online September 21, 2026. doi:10.1093/geront/gnag226.

Important new evidence•Peer-reviewed retrospective longitudinal cohort analysis•September 19, 2026

ADNI analysis separates GFAP signal from weak vascular markers

Across biomarker-specific ADNI samples, Simoa GFAP rose stepwise from cognitively unimpaired participants to MCI and Alzheimer disease and distinguished AD from unimpaired participants with AUC 0.822, while sTREM2 and the vascular markers showed substantial overlap and no individual-level diagnostic utility.

Key quantitative results: Baseline GFAP was 21.5% higher in MCI than cognitively unimpaired participants (95% CI 13.1%–30.6%) and 56.3% higher in AD (40.4%–74.2%; multiplicity-adjusted q=1.66×10⁻14). AD-versus-unimpaired discrimination was AUC 0.822 (95% CI 0.779–0.866), Cohen d=1.23, with distributional overlap of 0.51.

BiomarkersBloodGFAPsTREM2Disease characterization

Added September 20, 2026 · DOI:10.1096/fba.2026-00194; PMID:42763575; PMCID:PMC13589249

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

GFAP produced strong group-level separation, but this was a clinical-diagnosis analysis rather than an amyloid- or tau-defined diagnostic-validation study. sTREM2 was null at baseline, vascular-marker distributions overlapped heavily, and none of the measures was tested for clinical decision impact.

Study design

Secondary ADNI analysis of 2,650 covariate-complete participants: 1,027 cognitively unimpaired, 1,187 with mild cognitive impairment and 436 with Alzheimer disease. Baseline assay samples differed by platform: GFAP n=832, sTREM2 n=1,001 and vascular markers n=566. Longitudinal analyses included 1,252 participants and 1,671 GFAP observations, 1,031 participants and 1,771 sTREM2 observations, and 566 participants and 1,061 vascular-marker observations.

Key quantitative results

  • Baseline GFAP was 21.5% higher in MCI than cognitively unimpaired participants (95% CI 13.1%–30.6%) and 56.3% higher in AD (40.4%–74.2%; multiplicity-adjusted q=1.66×10⁻14). AD-versus-unimpaired discrimination was AUC 0.822 (95% CI 0.779–0.866), Cohen d=1.23, with distributional overlap of 0.51.
  • sTREM2 did not separate AD from unimpaired participants at baseline: +2.2% (95% CI −7.4% to 12.8%; q=0.769), AUC 0.507. VEGF and sVCAM-1 were modestly higher in AD, with AUCs of 0.612 and 0.625, while vascular-marker overlap was at least 0.83; sICAM-1 was not significant.
  • GFAP increased 4.50% per year in cognitively unimpaired participants (95% CI 3.79%–5.21%) and sTREM2 increased 2.99% per year (1.56%–4.44%), but diagnosis-by-time interactions were not significant after multiplicity correction. The vascular panel showed divergent 12-month patterns that require replication.

What changed

A single longitudinal ADNI analysis directly compared glial and vascular plasma markers across disease groups and quantified both group separation and longitudinal change on three assay platforms.

Strength of evidence

Moderate exploratory clinical-validity evidence from a large, well-characterized research cohort. Clinical groups were not defined against an amyloid or tau reference standard, assay availability was nonrandom and most GFAP and sTREM2 participants had only one measurement. The study provides no analytical-validation or clinical-utility evidence.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The findings support plasma GFAP as a research marker of glial activation with meaningful group-level separation, not as a stand-alone AD diagnostic or stage marker. The sTREM2 and vascular-marker findings do not support individual-level interpretation.

Field medical relevance

The study helps MSL teams distinguish a reproducible GFAP research signal from weaker exploratory vascular-marker findings and clarifies why diagnostic separation, assay validity and clinical utility should not be conflated.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The signals are assay- and dataset-specific. The study did not establish transferability across GFAP, sTREM2 or vascular-marker platforms, laboratories or cut points.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No assay authorization, commercial-availability, guideline-endorsement, coverage or reimbursement change follows from this analysis.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Was Alzheimer disease confirmed with amyloid or tau biomarkers?
No. The primary comparisons used clinical diagnosis groups, so the study does not establish AD-specific validity against a biological reference standard.
Did the study validate the assays analytically?
No. It analyzed existing platform-specific ADNI data and did not establish precision, interference, cross-platform equivalence or clinical cut points.
Can these markers be used for clinical decisions?
Not from this study. It did not test decision impact, patient outcomes, implementation thresholds or clinical utility.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Clinical diagnosis groups rather than an amyloid- or tau-defined reference standard
  • Retrospective secondary analysis with nonrandom and platform-specific assay availability
  • Most GFAP and sTREM2 participants contributed only one measurement
  • Vascular-marker follow-up was limited to 12 months and glial-vascular correlations used only 64 to 94 overlapping participants
  • No analytical validation, prospective decision-impact study or clinical-utility assessment

Primary source · DOI · PubMed Central full text · PubMed record

Jahanbin K; Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. Glial and Vascular Plasma Biomarkers Across the Alzheimer's Disease Continuum: An ADNI-Based Longitudinal Study. FASEB BioAdvances. Published online September 19, 2026. doi:10.1096/fba.2026-00194.

Implementation-relevant•Peer-reviewed retrospective imaging cohort•September 17, 2026

Cerebellar amyloid can bias florbetapir Centiloid quantification

In 359 amyloid-positive participants, cerebellar cortical amyloid raised the whole-cerebellum reference signal and could systematically underestimate cortical florbetapir burden; a white-matter-normalized cerebellar threshold showed strong internal discrimination but needs external validation.

Key quantitative results: Participants with cerebellar cortical amyloid had higher whole-cerebellum reference SUV (p=0.012) but lower cortical SUV (p=0.008), producing lower whole-cerebellum-referenced Centiloid estimates despite cortical amyloid burden; pons SUV did not differ significantly (p=0.110).

BiomarkersAmyloid PETAmyloidPET quantification

Added September 18, 2026 · DOI:10.1007/s00259-026-08140-6; PMID:42749937

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

Whole cerebellum is commonly treated as a stable reference region for amyloid PET, but this study shows that cerebellar amyloid can inflate the denominator and depress cortical SUVR and Centiloid values. The proposed screen may help identify affected scans, but it was derived and validated internally and is not a clinical cutoff.

Study design

Retrospective analysis of 359 amyloid-positive participants who had 18F-florbetapir PET, MRI and CSF biomarkers; 52 had visually defined cerebellar cortical amyloid deposition and 307 did not. A white-matter-normalized cerebellar SUVR threshold was derived and internally validated in 30 additional cases.

Key quantitative results

  • Participants with cerebellar cortical amyloid had higher whole-cerebellum reference SUV (p=0.012) but lower cortical SUV (p=0.008), producing lower whole-cerebellum-referenced Centiloid estimates despite cortical amyloid burden; pons SUV did not differ significantly (p=0.110).
  • A white-matter-normalized cerebellar SUVR threshold of 0.428 distinguished cerebellar deposition with AUC 0.931, 86.5% sensitivity and 86.3% specificity; internal validation in 30 cases yielded kappa 0.856.
  • In two lecanemab-treated cases, cortical Centiloid values declined longitudinally while cerebellar white-matter-normalized SUVR remained above the proposed threshold.

What changed

A dedicated analysis quantified a clinically relevant reference-region failure mode and proposed an internal screen for cerebellar amyloid before interpreting whole-cerebellum-referenced florbetapir measurements.

Strength of evidence

Moderate measurement-validity evidence: the cohort was sizeable and included internal validation, but all participants were already amyloid positive, only 52 had cerebellar deposition, validation included 30 cases and longitudinal treatment observations were limited to two people.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

When serial or borderline florbetapir measurements appear discordant with the cortical image pattern, cerebellar reference contamination should be considered before inferring low burden or treatment response. The proposed threshold is not ready for routine clinical decisions without external validation.

Field medical relevance

Useful for interpreting Centiloid values, selecting reference regions in trials and explaining why reference-region biology can alter quantitative amyloid PET results even when the tracer and cortical signal are unchanged.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The finding concerns reference-region selection and quantification of 18F-florbetapir PET. The 0.428 white-matter-normalized threshold should not be transferred to other tracers, scanners or processing pipelines without validation.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No authorization, commercial availability, formal guideline endorsement, coverage or reimbursement change follows from this study.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does this establish a new clinical cutoff?
No. The 0.428 threshold was derived and validated within the same research program and requires external, scanner- and pipeline-specific validation.
Should whole cerebellum no longer be used as a reference region?
Not categorically. The study identifies a subgroup in whom whole-cerebellum normalization may be biased; it does not compare all reference strategies prospectively or establish a universal replacement.
Does the study prove better clinical outcomes with another reference region?
No. It addresses measurement interpretation, not clinical utility or patient outcomes.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Retrospective, single-program analysis restricted to amyloid-positive participants
  • Only 52 participants had cerebellar cortical deposition
  • The proposed threshold had internal rather than independent external validation
  • Only two anti-amyloid-treated cases contributed longitudinal treatment examples
  • No prospective decision-impact or patient-outcome assessment

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record

Wang M, Bi S, Lu J, et al. Cerebellar cortical amyloid deposition biases 18F-Florbetapir PET quantification with whole cerebellum as reference region. Eur J Nucl Med Mol Imaging. Published online September 17, 2026. doi:10.1007/s00259-026-08140-6.

Important new evidence•Peer-reviewed methodological reanalysis•September 17, 2026

Reanalysis finds reported shingles-vaccine dementia effects internally implausible

After accounting for actual vaccine uptake, three of four published natural experiments implied dementia risk reductions of 84% to 177% among vaccine recipients, including estimates beyond the theoretical maximum, weakening the claim that these studies establish meaningful dementia prevention.

Key quantitative results: The implied dementia-risk reduction among vaccine recipients was 18% in Wales (95% CI approximately 0%–35%), 177% in Australia (28%–301%) and 84% (18%–219%) and 111% (15%–303%) in two Canadian analyses; two estimates exceeded the theoretical 100% maximum.

ManagementRisk reduction

Added September 18, 2026 · DOI:10.1016/j.bbi.2026.107021; PMID:42754179

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The paper does not test whether shingles vaccination has no effect on dementia. It shows that several highly publicized eligibility-based estimates become implausibly large when translated into effects among people actually vaccinated, suggesting residual bias or violated assumptions and a need for independent replication before prevention claims enter practice.

Study design

Reanalysis of published shingles-vaccine eligibility natural experiments from Wales, Australia and Canada. The investigators incorporated the observed difference in vaccination uptake across eligibility groups, calculated the treatment effect implied among vaccine recipients, tested the baseline-risk imbalance needed to reproduce the findings and inspected national dementia-incidence trends after vaccine introduction.

Key quantitative results

  • The implied dementia-risk reduction among vaccine recipients was 18% in Wales (95% CI approximately 0%–35%), 177% in Australia (28%–301%) and 84% (18%–219%) and 111% (15%–303%) in two Canadian analyses; two estimates exceeded the theoretical 100% maximum.
  • Even assuming a large true vaccine effect, baseline dementia risk in vaccine-eligible groups would need to be 1.7 to 2.3 times higher than in ineligible groups to generate the published eligibility contrasts.
  • The same framework implied 41% lower mild cognitive impairment and 56% lower dementia mortality, while national data did not show a corresponding post-rollout decline in dementia incidence in the United Kingdom, Australia or Canada.

What changed

A formal quantitative stress test translated published eligibility contrasts into recipient-level effects and showed that most were implausibly large or internally inconsistent.

Strength of evidence

Strong evidence about internal plausibility and identifying assumptions, but not a randomized estimate of vaccine effect. The analysis depends on published uptake and outcome data and cannot determine which specific bias produced each result.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Shingles vaccination should continue to follow infectious-disease recommendations, but it should not currently be presented as an established dementia-prevention intervention on the basis of these natural experiments.

Field medical relevance

Directly relevant to risk-reduction messaging, evidence appraisal and patient questions because the original studies have been interpreted as causal support for dementia prevention.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No authorization, vaccine availability, formal guideline endorsement, coverage or reimbursement change follows from this paper.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does this mean shingles vaccination cannot reduce dementia risk?
No. It shows that the published natural-experiment estimates are not internally credible as strong causal evidence. A smaller effect remains possible and requires independent replication.
Does this change shingles-vaccine recommendations?
No. The paper does not change vaccination indications or guidance for preventing herpes zoster and its complications.
Is this a clinical trial or guideline?
No. It is a methodological reanalysis of observational natural experiments.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Reanalysis of published observational studies rather than participant-level randomized data
  • Cannot identify the exact source or magnitude of bias in each original study
  • National incidence trends are ecological and may be influenced by diagnostic and demographic changes
  • Does not estimate a definitive vaccine effect on dementia

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record

Kivimäki M, et al. Natural experiments of herpes zoster vaccination: Quantifying the implied vaccine effectiveness against dementia. Brain Behav Immun. Published online September 17, 2026. doi:10.1016/j.bbi.2026.107021.

Important new evidence•ClinicalTrials.gov results record•September 17, 2026

Two-year nicotine patch trial finds no cognitive benefit in MCI

In 348 adults with mild cognitive impairment, 24 months of transdermal nicotine did not improve the prespecified verbal-memory outcome versus placebo and caused more dizziness and treatment withdrawals; the newly posted registry results do not support clinical use.

Key quantitative results: For the primary International Shopping List Test immediate-recall outcome at month 24, least-squares means were 16.95 with nicotine and 16.59 with placebo; adjusted mean difference 0.37 points (95% CI −0.78 to 1.52; p=0.530). A complier analysis was also null (difference 0.12, 95% CI −1.27 to 1.51; p=0.868).

Registry ResultsManagementMild cognitive impairment

Added September 18, 2026 · NCT02720445; ClinicalTrials.gov results first posted 2026-09-17

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The official registry now supplies exact 24-month effect estimates for a long-running trial of an inexpensive, readily available intervention. Neither the primary memory outcome nor global, functional or cognitive secondary measures showed a convincing benefit, and attrition and adverse effects limit enthusiasm for off-label use.

Study design

Forty-one-site phase 2 trial that randomized 348 nonsmoking adults with mild cognitive impairment to transdermal nicotine (titrated from 3.5 mg to 21 mg daily) or placebo for 24 months, with quadruple masking and a three-week taper.

Key quantitative results

  • For the primary International Shopping List Test immediate-recall outcome at month 24, least-squares means were 16.95 with nicotine and 16.59 with placebo; adjusted mean difference 0.37 points (95% CI −0.78 to 1.52; p=0.530). A complier analysis was also null (difference 0.12, 95% CI −1.27 to 1.51; p=0.868).
  • Secondary estimates were similarly inconclusive: delayed recall difference 0.16 (95% CI −0.45 to 0.74), CDR-SB −0.09 (−0.50 to 0.32), ADCS-ADL −0.05 (−1.79 to 1.68) and post-hoc MMSE 0.61 (−0.14 to 1.35).
  • Completion was 91/171 with nicotine and 106/177 with placebo. Adverse-event withdrawal occurred in 28 versus 17 participants; dizziness occurred in 29/171 versus 8/176, headache in 13/171 versus 4/176, insomnia in 13/171 versus 5/176 and abnormal dreams in 12/171 versus 2/176. Serious adverse events occurred in 27/171 versus 24/176, with one death in each arm.

What changed

Detailed results were first posted to ClinicalTrials.gov on September 17, 2026, supplying exact 24-month efficacy, attrition and safety data beyond earlier topline reporting.

Strength of evidence

Randomized, masked, multicenter evidence with 24 months of treatment, but the result is currently registry-based and attrition was substantial, with only 91 nicotine and 106 placebo participants completing follow-up.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The posted evidence does not support transdermal nicotine as a treatment for mild cognitive impairment and identifies a meaningful tolerability and discontinuation burden.

Field medical relevance

Useful for counseling about an accessible off-label intervention, for closing the loop on prior pilot signals and for informing whether additional nicotine studies should proceed without a stronger target-population or dosing rationale.

Access or reimbursement relevance

Transdermal nicotine is commercially available, but this study establishes no MCI indication, guideline endorsement, coverage policy or reason for unsupervised use.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Is this a newly published clinical-trial paper?
No. The qualifying development is the official results posting in ClinicalTrials.gov, so it is categorized as Registry Results rather than Clinical Trials.
Should patients with MCI try nicotine patches?
These results do not support that use. Nicotine also caused more dizziness and treatment withdrawals, and it has no established MCI treatment indication.
Was an Alzheimer biomarker used to select participants?
The registry result is not a central biomarker report and is not tagged Biomarkers.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Results are currently reported in the registry rather than a peer-reviewed primary manuscript
  • Substantial attrition over 24 months, with differential adverse-event withdrawals
  • The MCI population was not defined by a central Alzheimer biomarker question
  • Multiple secondary and post-hoc outcomes do not overcome the null prespecified primary result

Primary source · Structured registry record

Vanderbilt University Medical Center. Memory Improvement Through Nicotine Dosing (MIND) Study. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02720445. Results first posted September 17, 2026.

Implementation-relevant•Peer-reviewed cross-sectional content analysis•September 15, 2026

Social media posts often overstate Alzheimer blood-test screening utility

Among 188 high-reach social-media posts, 36% promoted Alzheimer blood tests for asymptomatic screening, but only 12% of those posts mentioned potential harms; the study supports stronger communication guardrails, not broader testing.

Key quantitative results: Sixty-eight of 188 posts (36%) claimed utility for screening asymptomatic people; only 8 of those 68 (12%) mentioned potential harms.

BiomarkersBloodAlzheimer disease blood biomarkersTest interpretation

Added September 16, 2026 · DOI:10.1111/jgs.70692

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The study identifies a recurring implementation hazard as blood-based Alzheimer testing becomes more available: public-facing claims often blur symptomatic diagnostic evaluation with asymptomatic screening and omit harms, uncertainty, and the clinician's role. It evaluates communication quality, not assay performance or clinical utility.

Study design

Researchers searched Facebook, Instagram and TikTok in April 2025, screened 342 posts, excluded 30 after eligibility review and analyzed 188 English-language posts published from March 2014 through May 2025. The accounts had a combined potential reach of 114,043,984 followers.

Key quantitative results

  • Sixty-eight of 188 posts (36%) claimed utility for screening asymptomatic people; only 8 of those 68 (12%) mentioned potential harms.
  • One hundred eleven posts (59%) claimed earlier or improved diagnosis, but only 15 (14%) mentioned objective cognitive decline, 19 (17%) subjective cognitive decline and 20 (18%) a clinician's role.
  • Sixty-eight posts (36%) mentioned evidence, and only 16 of those 68 (24%) cited a specific identifiable study. Accounts with an explicit financial interest were more likely to claim asymptomatic-screening utility (odds ratio 3.38, 95% CI 1.59–7.22).

What changed

A first-of-its-kind content analysis quantified how Alzheimer blood tests are represented to a very large potential social-media audience and identified specific omissions relevant to test counseling and responsible implementation.

Strength of evidence

Direct, systematically coded evidence about public communication across three platforms, with duplicate coding and quantitative comparisons; it does not measure actual exposure, patient behavior, diagnostic accuracy or clinical outcomes.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Clinicians and field teams should anticipate that patients may arrive with expectations shaped by claims about screening healthy people. Counseling should clearly distinguish symptomatic diagnostic use from unsupported population screening and address false positives, overdiagnosis, uncertainty and the need for clinical assessment.

Field medical relevance

Useful for medical-information review, educational-material design and implementation planning because it identifies the claims most likely to create misunderstanding as blood tests enter practice.

Quanterix or platform relevance

No named assay or platform was evaluated. The findings should not be used to compare products, infer analytical or clinical validity, or transfer claims across blood-biomarker platforms.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No authorization, commercial availability, formal guideline endorsement, coverage or reimbursement change follows from this study.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does this study show that Alzheimer blood tests are inaccurate?
No. It did not evaluate analytical validity or clinical validity; it evaluated claims and contextual information in social-media posts.
Does it establish clinical utility for asymptomatic screening?
No. The authors highlight that posts frequently promoted asymptomatic screening despite the lack of established benefit and the potential for harm.
Is this a guideline or regulatory action?
No. It is an observational communication study and does not change authorization, availability, guideline endorsement, coverage or reimbursement.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Cross-sectional snapshot shaped by April 2025 platform search results and algorithms
  • English-language posts only, spanning March 2014 to May 2025
  • Follower counts represent potential reach rather than verified engagement or patient behavior
  • The study does not evaluate assay performance, diagnostic outcomes, clinical utility or patient outcomes

Primary source · DOI

Sujana RS, McCaffery KJ, Smith J, et al. Social media claims about blood tests for Alzheimer's disease and dementia: a cross-sectional content analysis. J Am Geriatr Soc. Published online September 15, 2026. doi:10.1111/jgs.70692.

Important new evidence•Peer-reviewed longitudinal cohort study•September 11, 2026

Longitudinal CSF pathology and cognitive resilience jointly predicted Alzheimer dementia

In 3,119 older adults followed for a median 13.7 years, a longitudinal CSF p-tau181/Aβ42 pathology score and a model-derived cognitive-resilience score independently predicted incident Alzheimer dementia, but neither score is validated for individual clinical decisions.

Key quantitative results: Each 1-SD higher longitudinal CSF pathology score was associated with incident Alzheimer dementia (HR 2.50, 95% CI 2.30–2.72).

BiomarkersCSFCSF p-tau181/Aβ42Prognosis

Added September 12, 2026 · DOI:10.1038/s41591-026-04635-9; NCT03653156

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The study is useful because it shows that longitudinal CSF pathology and observed cognitive trajectory contribute complementary prognostic information. It does not establish a deployable score, a treatment threshold, or evidence that an intervention that raises the model-derived resilience score will reduce dementia risk.

Study design

Landmark analysis of 3,119 older adults in the China Cognition and Aging Study with repeated CSF and cognitive measurements over a five-year score-estimation window and median follow-up of 13.7 years; findings were replicated in 597 ADNI participants with 133 incident events.

Key quantitative results

  • Each 1-SD higher longitudinal CSF pathology score was associated with incident Alzheimer dementia (HR 2.50, 95% CI 2.30–2.72).
  • Each 1-SD higher model-derived cognitive-resilience score was associated with lower incidence (HR 0.51, 95% CI 0.48–0.55).
  • The ADNI replication included 597 participants and 133 incident events; the authors reported independent pathology and resilience associations and a multiplicative interaction.

What changed

A large, long-followed cohort analysis paired repeated CSF pathology measurements with longitudinal cognitive trajectory and showed that the two dimensions provided complementary prognostic information, with replication in ADNI.

Strength of evidence

Moderate prognostic evidence: large longitudinal derivation cohort, long follow-up and independent replication, but both scores were research-derived and the resilience measure is a model residual that can include measurement error and unmeasured determinants.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The findings support considering clinical resilience alongside pathology in research and trial design. They do not justify serial lumbar punctures, individual risk counseling from these scores, or a specific resilience-directed intervention.

Field medical relevance

Useful for questions about why similar biomarker burdens produce different clinical trajectories and whether pathology alone is sufficient for prognosis. The answer remains no, but the proposed joint model is not ready for routine use.

Quanterix or platform relevance

No platform comparison or transferable threshold was established. The public report does not support applying the model to a different CSF assay or to plasma p-tau measurements.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No authorization, availability, guideline endorsement, coverage, or reimbursement change follows from this prognostic cohort study.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Can the pathology and resilience scores be used in clinic now?
No. They were derived retrospectively from repeated research measurements and have no validated clinical cutoff or decision-impact evidence.
Does the study prove that increasing cognitive resilience prevents Alzheimer dementia?
No. Cognitive resilience was a model-derived residual, not a randomized intervention target. The association is prognostic, not proof of causal benefit.
Does the study establish assay performance?
No. It evaluates prognostic associations of a longitudinal CSF ratio, not analytical validity, assay interchangeability, or platform-specific thresholds.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Research-derived scores without validated clinical cutoffs
  • Resilience defined as a residual that may contain measurement error and unmeasured influences
  • Repeated CSF sampling limits routine-care feasibility
  • No clinical-utility or intervention trial
  • Publicly accessible report does not establish analytical validity or assay interchangeability

Primary source · DOI

Wang Z, Wang S, Liang Y, et al. Joint impact of pathological burden and cognitive resilience on Alzheimer's disease risk. Nat Med. Published online September 11, 2026. doi:10.1038/s41591-026-04635-9.

Early signal•ClinicalTrials.gov results record•September 8, 2026

Ketogenic diet trial posts inconclusive 12-week cognitive results

Registry results showed small, imprecise within-group ADAS-Cog changes and more nonserious adverse events with the ketogenic diet; no between-group effect estimate was reported.

Key quantitative results: For the primary ADAS-Cog11 outcome, mean change was −0.52 points (95% CI −2.85 to 1.81; n=32) with ketogenic diet and +0.96 (95% CI −1.04 to 2.97; n=37) with the comparator; lower scores are better, and the registry reports no between-group estimate.

Registry ResultsManagementNonpharmacologic care

Added September 8, 2026 · NCT03860792; ClinicalTrials.gov results first posted 2026-09-08

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The registry results are insufficient to recommend a ketogenic diet as an AD cognitive treatment, particularly without a reported between-group estimate.

Study design

Eighty-four adults aged 50–90 with Alzheimer disease and CDR 0.5 or 1 were randomized 1:1 to a 12-week ketogenic diet or Therapeutic Lifestyle Changes diet; outcome assessors were masked.

Key quantitative results

  • For the primary ADAS-Cog11 outcome, mean change was −0.52 points (95% CI −2.85 to 1.81; n=32) with ketogenic diet and +0.96 (95% CI −1.04 to 2.97; n=37) with the comparator; lower scores are better, and the registry reports no between-group estimate.
  • Completion was 32/42 versus 38/42. Nonserious adverse events affected 17/42 versus 9/42, including diarrhea in 9/42 versus 0/42; no serious events or deaths were reported in either group.

What changed

Primary results were first posted to ClinicalTrials.gov on September 8, 2026.

Strength of evidence

Randomized evidence, but small, short, incompletely analyzed and currently registry-only, with no reported between-group treatment effect.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The posted results do not establish cognitive benefit from a ketogenic diet in mild AD and identify a meaningful tolerability burden.

Field medical relevance

Supports careful counseling about uncertain cognitive benefit, adherence demands and gastrointestinal effects when patients ask about ketogenic diets.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No authorization, formal guideline endorsement, commercial availability or coverage change is established.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Do these results prove that ketogenic diets have no benefit?
No. The 12-week trial is small and the registry does not report a between-group estimate, so the result is inconclusive rather than definitive.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Fourteen randomized participants did not complete the study, with more withdrawals in the ketogenic group.
  • The registry reports arm-specific change estimates but no adjusted between-group comparison, and no peer-reviewed primary results publication was identified.

Primary source · Structured registry record

University of Kansas Medical Center. Therapeutic Diets in Alzheimer's Disease (TDAD). ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03860792. Results first posted September 8, 2026.

GuidelinesManagementRisk reduction

Added September 7, 2026 · WHO ISBN 978-92-4-012355-7

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

This is guidance for normal cognition and MCI, not evidence that established AD dementia can be reversed.

Evidence basis and population

WHO evidence synthesis for adults without dementia, with a life-course and public-health focus.

Key recommendations

Clinical TrialsManagementCSFTotal tauTau PETDisease-modifying treatment

Added September 7, 2026 · NCT05399888

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The primary endpoint failed, and favorable secondary comparisons require confirmation.

Study design

CELIA randomized 416 anti-amyloid-naive participants with MCI or mild AD dementia to intrathecal diranersen or placebo for 18 months.

Key quantitative results

  • At 60 mg every 6 months (n=60) versus placebo (n=115), the reported CDR-SB difference was −0.54 points, or 26% less decline. Confidence intervals were not supplied in the cited release.
  • The 115 mg regimens showed smaller CDR-SB differences (−0.28 and −0.18); ADCS-ADL-MCI did not separate from placebo.

What changed

July data quantify the earlier topline announcement.

Strength of evidence

Randomized design, but conference/sponsor reporting with a failed primary endpoint.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Insufficient for clinical use.

Field medical relevance

Keep nominal secondary findings separate from confirmatory evidence.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Tau reduction does not establish an assay’s clinical utility.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No approval, availability or coverage claim.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Was the study positive on its primary endpoint?
No. Dose response on CDR-SB was not demonstrated.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Multiplicity, small lowest-dose group, and absent confidence intervals.
  • Full independent peer-reviewed assessment was not verified.

Lecanemab labeling adds subcutaneous treatment initiation

The July label permits weekly subcutaneous initiation, extending home-injection options beyond maintenance treatment.

Key label details: Subcutaneous starting dose is 500 mg weekly, as two 250 mg injections. After 18 months, continuing that regimen or transitioning to maintenance is permitted.

ManagementDisease-modifying treatment

Added September 7, 2026 · BLA 761375/S-001; FDA label reference 5833017

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

Route convenience changes delivery planning, while amyloid confirmation, early symptomatic eligibility and ARIA precautions remain.

Study design

Label update for initiation in MCI or mild AD dementia, with confirmed amyloid pathology.

Key label details

  • Subcutaneous starting dose is 500 mg weekly, as two 250 mg injections. After 18 months, continuing that regimen or transitioning to maintenance is permitted.
  • Subcutaneous maintenance is 360 mg weekly. The label specifies baseline MRI and monitoring after 1, 2, 3 and 6 months.

What changed

Subcutaneous dosing can begin at treatment initiation.

Strength of evidence

Authoritative dosing instructions; not a new head-to-head clinical-benefit trial.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Initiation and maintenance strengths must remain distinct.

Field medical relevance

Discuss delivery burden together with safety infrastructure.

Access or reimbursement relevance

FDA authorization is verified. Current supply, coverage and patient cost are not established here.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does home dosing remove ARIA monitoring?
No. The boxed warning and MRI surveillance still apply.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • This route change does not establish superior cognition outcomes or lower ARIA risk.
  • APOE ε4 homozygotes face higher ARIA risk; consult genotype counseling and risk instructions.
